subject: Mathematics
learning_objectives: Understand what an equation is and how it differs from an expression
Identify the LHS (left hand side), RHS (right hand side), and the variable in an equation
Solve simple linear equations in one variable using the balancing method
Solve equations using the transposing method
Set up equations from word problems and solve them
Verify solutions by substituting back into the original equation
Understand that the same operation applied to both sides preserves equality
prerequisite_knowledge: Knowledge of variables and algebraic expressions from earlier classes
Understanding of the four operations on integers
Basic understanding of LHS and RHS in mathematical statements
Concept of equality — that both sides of '=' must represent the same value

introduction.why_important: Equations are the language of mathematics applied to real-world problem solving. Almost every real-life problem — calculating age, distance, price, time — can be set up as an equation and solved systematically. Algebra, calculus, physics, engineering, economics — all rest on the foundation of equation-solving.
introduction.real_life_relevance: If you earn ₹x per day and ₹1,500 in 5 days, then 5x = 1500 → x = ₹300/day. If a rectangular field has perimeter 48 m and length is 3 more than width, you can set up and solve an equation to find the dimensions. Equations turn guesswork into certainty.
introduction.karnataka_context: A Bengaluru IT professional calculates project timelines using equations. A Mysuru silk weaver calculates thread required using equations. A Karnataka farmer computes fertiliser quantity per acre using simple equations. Even splitting a restaurant bill in Bengaluru uses equation thinking: 'if 4 people pay equal shares and one coupon reduces total by ₹200, what does each person pay?'
introduction.connection_to_previous_learning: Class VI introduced expressions and variables. Class VII introduces the equation — an expression with an equality sign — and the systematic method for finding the value of the unknown variable that makes the equation true.

characters.name: Variable (x, y, n…)
characters.role: The unknown quantity we are trying to find — represents a number we don't yet know

characters.name: Equation
characters.role: A mathematical statement that two expressions are equal — contains an '=' sign and a variable

characters.name: The Balance Method
characters.role: Treating the equation as a balance scale — whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other to keep it balanced

characters.name: Transposition
characters.role: Moving a term from one side of the equation to the other, changing its sign — a shortcut for the balance method

plot: The chapter opens with a puzzle: 'I think of a number, add 5 to it, and get 12. What is the number?' This sets up: x + 5 = 12.
It introduces the concept of an equation — a statement asserting equality between two expressions — and defines LHS, RHS, and variable.
It develops the balancing method: an equation is like a balance scale; performing the same operation on both sides maintains equality.
It shows how to solve equations: x + 5 = 12 → subtract 5 from both sides → x = 7.
It introduces the transposing method as a shortcut: moving a term to the other side changes its sign.
It solves progressively complex equations: linear equations with variables on one side, then with variables and constants on both sides.
It develops word problems — translating English sentences into equations and solving them.
The chapter closes by emphasising verification — always substitute the answer back into the original equation to confirm.
story_summary.moral: An equation is a puzzle with a unique solution. The balancing method provides a systematic, reliable way to solve any linear equation. Checking your answer by substitution is not optional — it is the mathematical proof that your answer is correct.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal, connected by an '=' sign. It contains at least one variable (unknown). An expression does NOT have an '=' sign; an equation DOES.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Expression vs Equation: '3x + 5' is an EXPRESSION (no equals sign). '3x + 5 = 14' is an EQUATION (has equals sign). Components: LHS (Left Hand Side) = the expression to the left of '='. RHS (Right Hand Side) = the expression to the right. Variable = the unknown (x, y, n, etc.). Solution = the value of the variable that makes LHS = RHS. Example: In 2x − 3 = 7: LHS = 2x−3, RHS = 7, Variable = x. Solution: 2(5)−3 = 7 ✓ → x=5 is the solution. An equation is like a balance scale — both sides weigh the same. Disturbing one side without doing the same to the other breaks the balance.
core_concepts.real_life_example: 'I think of a number, double it, and subtract 4 to get 10.' Equation: 2x − 4 = 10. Here x is the mystery number. Solving: 2x = 14, x = 7. Check: 2(7)−4 = 14−4 = 10 ✓.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: 'A Bengaluru auto driver charges ₹15 for the first km and ₹11 per km after that. A passenger pays ₹48. How many km did they travel after the first km?' Equation: 15 + 11n = 48 → 11n = 33 → n = 3 km.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students confuse expressions with equations. '2x+3' is NOT an equation — you cannot 'solve' it because there is no equals sign. Only equations can be solved. Also, students sometimes think an equation can have any number of solutions — a simple linear equation in one variable has exactly ONE solution.
core_concepts.memory_tip: Equation = EQUAL (has = sign). Expression = just a phrase (no = sign). 'Equation has an EQUAL sign. Expression is just an expression — it expresses a value but makes no claim about what it equals.' E = equation = equal sign present.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: Balancing: perform the same operation on both sides to isolate the variable. Transposing: move a term to the other side, changing its sign. Both methods give the same result.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Balancing Method: Goal = get the variable alone on one side. Rule = whatever you do to one side, do exactly the same to the other. Examples: x + 8 = 15 → subtract 8 from both sides → x = 7. 3x = 21 → divide both sides by 3 → x = 7. 2x − 5 = 11 → add 5 to both sides → 2x = 16 → divide by 2 → x = 8. Transposing Method (shortcut): when a term moves to the other side, its sign changes. Addition becomes subtraction; subtraction becomes addition; multiplication becomes division; division becomes multiplication. Example: x + 8 = 15 → x = 15 − 8 = 7 (8 'transposed' to RHS, sign changed from + to −). 3x = 21 → x = 21/3 = 7 (3 'transposed', × becomes ÷). Complex: 2x + 3 = x + 7 → 2x − x = 7 − 3 → x = 4.
core_concepts.real_life_example: A shopkeeper has some apples (x). After selling 23 and buying 15 more, he has 42. Equation: x − 23 + 15 = 42 → x − 8 = 42 → x = 50. He started with 50 apples. Verify: 50 − 23 + 15 = 27 + 15 = 42 ✓.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Ravi and his sister together have ₹240. Ravi has ₹30 more than his sister. Find each person's amount. Let sister's amount = x. Ravi's = x+30. Equation: x + (x+30) = 240 → 2x + 30 = 240 → 2x = 210 → x = 105. Sister: ₹105, Ravi: ₹135. Check: 105+135 = 240 ✓.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students sometimes transpose incorrectly — forgetting to change the sign. If 'x + 5 = 12' and they write 'x = 12 + 5 = 17' — that is WRONG (5 should become −5 on the other side). Always: when you MOVE a term across the '=' sign, FLIP its sign. Also, students forget to verify — always substitute the answer back to check.
core_concepts.memory_tip: TRANSPOSE = MOVE and CHANGE SIGN. + becomes −, − becomes +, × becomes ÷, ÷ becomes ×. Think of 'teleporting' a term — it arrives on the other side in opposite form. Verify ALWAYS: substitute x back and check LHS = RHS.

core_concepts.concept_name: Setting Up Equations from Word Problems
core_concepts.simple_explanation: Translate English statements into mathematical equations by identifying the unknown (variable), the relationship between quantities, and expressing that relationship as an equation. Then solve and verify.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Steps for word problems: (1) READ carefully — identify what is unknown. (2) ASSIGN — let the unknown = x (or any variable). (3) TRANSLATE — convert the English conditions into an equation using mathematical operations. (4) SOLVE — use balancing or transposing. (5) VERIFY — substitute back and check. (6) STATE THE ANSWER — answer the question asked, with units. Key translation phrases: 'sum' = addition, 'difference' = subtraction, 'product' = multiplication, 'quotient' = division, 'exceeds by' = adds to, 'twice' = 2×, 'thrice' = 3×, 'is' or 'equals' = '='.
core_concepts.real_life_example: The sum of three consecutive integers is 72. Let the integers be n, n+1, n+2. Equation: n + (n+1) + (n+2) = 72 → 3n + 3 = 72 → 3n = 69 → n = 23. Integers: 23, 24, 25. Check: 23+24+25 = 72 ✓.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: A Karnataka farmer has a rectangular field. Its length is twice its breadth. Its perimeter is 120 m. Find the dimensions. Let breadth = x. Length = 2x. Perimeter = 2(l+b) = 2(2x+x) = 6x = 120 → x = 20 m. Breadth = 20 m, Length = 40 m. Check: 2(40+20) = 2×60 = 120 m ✓.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students struggle with 'consecutive integers' — remember they are n, n+1, n+2 (not n, 2n, 3n). Also, 'a number is 5 more than another' means x+5 (not 5x). Carefully read: 'twice a number' = 2x, but 'a number twice' means the same thing. Always define what x represents before writing the equation.
core_concepts.memory_tip: Word problem steps: READ → ASSIGN x → TRANSLATE to equation → SOLVE → VERIFY → ANSWER. 'RATS-VA': Read, Assign, Translate, Solve, Verify, Answer. Never skip the Verify step — it proves your answer is correct.

key_terms_glossary.meaning: A mathematical statement asserting that two expressions are equal, connected by an '=' sign. Contains at least one variable. Example: 3x + 2 = 11.
A mathematical phrase consisting of numbers, variables, and operations — but WITHOUT an equals sign. Example: 3x + 2. Expressions cannot be 'solved'; equations can.
A symbol (usually a letter like x, y, or n) that represents an unknown or changing quantity in an equation.
The expression to the left of the equals sign in an equation. In 2x + 3 = 11, the LHS is '2x + 3'.
The expression to the right of the equals sign in an equation. In 2x + 3 = 11, the RHS is '11'.
The value of the variable that makes both sides of the equation equal. Also called the 'root' of the equation. Example: x = 4 is the solution of 2x + 3 = 11.
A method of solving equations by performing the same mathematical operation on both sides to maintain equality, ultimately isolating the variable.
Moving a term from one side of an equation to the other, changing its sign in the process. Addition becomes subtraction; multiplication becomes division.
An equation where the highest power of the variable is 1. Example: 3x + 2 = 11 is linear. 3x² + 2 = 11 is NOT linear (x has power 2).
The process of checking that the solution is correct by substituting the value of the variable back into the original equation and confirming LHS = RHS.

worked_examples.question: Solve: 4x − 3 = 13
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: Add 3 to both sides (to eliminate −3 from LHS).

worked_examples.question: The sum of two consecutive even numbers is 74. Find the numbers.
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: Let the first even number = x. Next consecutive even number = x + 2.

worked_examples.question: Sachin's age is 3 times his son's age. 10 years later, Sachin will be twice his son's age. Find their present ages.
step_by_step_answer: Let son's present age = x. Sachin's present age = 3x.
Son's age = 10 years. Sachin's age = 30 years.
Verify: After 10 years: Son=20, Sachin=40. Is 40 = 2×20? Yes ✓.

quick_check_questions.after_concept: Simple Equations — Balancing, Transposing, Word Problems

questions.q: What is the difference between an expression and an equation?
questions.a: An expression has no '=' sign (e.g., 3x+5). An equation has an '=' sign and states that two expressions are equal (e.g., 3x+5 = 14). Only equations can be solved.

questions.q: A number when multiplied by 4 and then reduced by 6 gives 18. Find the number.
Why must you verify the solution of an equation?
questions.a: Verification confirms the solution is correct. If LHS ≠ RHS after substituting, there is a calculation error. It is the mathematical proof of correctness.

key_takeaways: An equation has an '=' sign; an expression does not. Only equations can be solved.
LHS = left of '='; RHS = right of '='; variable = unknown to be found.
Balancing method: perform the same operation on both sides to isolate the variable.
Transposing: move a term to the other side and change its sign (+ ↔ −, × ↔ ÷).
Steps to solve: isolate the variable, simplify, find x.
Always verify: substitute the solution back into the original equation and check LHS = RHS.
Word problems: Read → Assign variable → Translate → Solve → Verify → State answer.
Consecutive integers: n, n+1, n+2. Consecutive even/odd: n, n+2, n+4.
A linear equation in one variable has exactly ONE solution.

revision_notes: Chapter 4 — Simple Equations. Equation = mathematical statement with '=' sign containing a variable. Expression = no '=' sign. LHS = left of '='; RHS = right. Variable = unknown (x, y, n). Balancing method: same operation on both sides to isolate variable. Transposing: move term across '=', change sign (+ → −, × → ÷). Solving: add/subtract to remove constants, multiply/divide to remove coefficients. Verification: substitute answer back — LHS must equal RHS. Word problems: Assign variable → write equation → solve → verify → answer. Key phrases: sum(+), difference(−), twice(2x), 'is'(=), 'exceeds by n'(+n). Consecutive integers: n, n+1, n+2. Consecutive evens/odds: n, n+2, n+4. Linear equation in one variable has exactly one solution.
must_remember_facts: Equation = has '=' sign. Expression = no '=' sign. Only equations are solved.
Balancing: do the SAME operation to BOTH sides.
Transposing: term moves to other side → sign changes (+ → −, × → ÷).
To solve ax + b = c: transpose b → ax = c−b; divide by a → x = (c−b)/a.
Verification: substitute x back. If LHS = RHS → correct. If not → error.
Word problems: Read, Assign (let x = ?), Translate (write equation), Solve, Verify.
Consecutive integers: n, n+1, n+2. Their sum = 3n+3.
Consecutive even/odd integers: n, n+2, n+4. Their sum = 3n+6.
A simple linear equation in one variable has exactly ONE unique solution.
